chunks.text: Dalbergia sissoo, first described by William Roxburgh, belongs to the pea family Fabaceae. It is native to the foothills of the Himalayas, ranging from Afghanistan in the west across to Bihar in eastern India, and also occurs naturally in Iran. It typically grows along riverbanks above 200 m elevation, up to about 1,400 m, and tolerates a wide range of conditions — from near-freezing temperatures to nearly 50°C, up to 2,000 mm of annual rainfall, and droughts of three to four months. It is a medium to large deciduous tree reaching up to 25 m in height and 2–3 m in trunk diameter (though usually smaller in open cultivation), with leathery, alternate, pinnately compound leaves about 15 cm long, whitish-to-pink fragrant flowers, and flat, strap-shaped pods holding one to five seeds.

Shisham is regarded, after teak, as one of the most important cultivated timber trees of India (historically described as Bihar's most important cultivated timber). Its heartwood ranges from golden to dark brown and is prized for its strength and rich grain, used widely in furniture, veneer, musical instruments and plywood, while the paler sapwood is used more incidentally. The tree also shows excellent coppicing ability, which makes it well suited to fuelwood cultivation on 10–15 year rotation cycles. Traditional medicinal uses include applying seed oil or powdered wood to skin ailments, and folk use for stomach and blood conditions, though these are traditional rather than clinically established uses. Its leaves and young sprouts serve as valuable winter fodder for livestock and for monkeys.

Ecologically, the species is the larval host plant for the black rajah butterfly (Charaxes solon). It is the state tree of Punjab. Its heartwood contains a distinctive neoflavonoid compound called dalbergichromene.
